text: DERM is a Class III CE-marked AI medical device.

Screening, triage, and assessment of cutaneous lesions suspicious for skin cancer to help route non-cancerous lesions away from cancer pathways and conserve specialist capacity. Dermoscopic images captured with approved hardware (camera device, dermoscope, and connection kit, typically a smartphone with an attachment). Suspected diagnosis and referral/management recommendation; outputs can include management instructions such as refer, discharge, or monitor, and lesion class labels (e.g., possible melanoma, probable BCC). Autonomous AI medical device capable of issuing management instructions such as discharge without a second clinician read for labeled use cases; can also augment clinician decision-making. Primary care and secondary care clinicians are intended users of DERM outputs in pathway deployments; image capture may involve photographers or patients, but output interpretation is for trained clinical users. Patients aged 18 years or over with cutaneous lesions where there is suspicion of skin cancer, in any body location except where specific exclusions apply.

Should not be used on patients under 18; for non-cancer skin conditions; for treatment monitoring or staging; or on non-dermoscopic images. Contraindications include open/ulcerated lesions, lesions obscured by hair/tattoos/scars, lesions beneath nails, in eyes, on mucosal surfaces, on soles/palms, and previously biopsied lesions. DERM does not provide a definitive skin-cancer diagnosis. Manufacturer headline metrics and pathway evaluations should be interpreted alongside study-specific endpoints; evaluation has primarily been on Fitzpatrick I–IV, and some prospective cohorts are heavily skewed toward lighter phototypes.

Artificial intelligence algorithms — Deep Ensemble for the Recognition of Malignancy (DERM). Developed in accordance with Skin Analytics’ ISO 13485:2016 certified Quality Management System and fulfills UK/EU medical-device regulatory provisions described in the IFU. NCT04116983 (DERM-003 / NMSC validation). NCT04123678 (DERM-005 / health-economics / teledermatology pathway study). NCT05126173 (DERM-006 / US and EU validation).

Manufacturer communications report DERM achieving a 99.8% accuracy rate in ruling out cancer, compared with 98.9% typically attributed to dermatologists in that same communication. An NHS AI in Health and Care Award evaluation reported high pathway sensitivity for malignant melanoma (97%). A Skin Analytics news summary of a prospective study reported that DERM could identify melanoma with similar accuracy to skin cancer specialists in a study of over 1,500 lesions.
Primarily evaluated on Fitzpatrick skin types I–IV; use caution on other skin types.

DERM (Deep Ensemble for the Recognition of Malignancy), which is SkinAnalytics' Class III CE marked AI as a Medical Device (AIaMD), is built around the company's custom teledermatology platform to help triage patients to the right place, at the right time to use dermatologist resources most efficiently. DERM assesses dermoscopic images of skin lesions submitted by primary care and dermatologists seeing patients and gives a suspected diagnosis along with a referral recommendation based on the suspected diagnosis. This ensures patients with non-cancerous lesions are safely triaged away from cancer pathways to make space for patients who need them.

DERM is an AI-based skin lesion analysis device intended for use in the screening, triage and assessment of skin lesions suspicious for skin cancer. DERM analyzes dermoscopic images of skin lesions and gives a suspected diagnosis, and relevant referral recommendation. This helps ensure that patients with non-cancerous lesions are not sent down cancer pathways and dermatologist resources are used most effectively. Physicians, including primary care doctors and dermatologists, submit dermatoscopic images of lesions suspicious for cancer from patients they are evaluating. Dermoscopic images must be captured using approved dermoscopy devices. SkinAnalytics is integrated with physicians' teledermatology and EHR systems via API for image submission, result delivery, and automated clinical workflow triggers. Structured clinical assessment and referral guidance: for each lesion assessment, the results returned by DERM include the suspected diagnosis, referral recommendation, referral recommendation guidance, and analysis explanation. DERM completes image analysis in less than 20 seconds using the DERM AI model trained on skin lesion data. Users may use DERM and its outputs as an automated clinical management tool or to augment other clinical data points to support clinical decision-making. DERM is intended to be used by primary care clinicians/providers and specialty care providers (e.g. dermatologists). Necessary knowledge/expertise: clinical training in skin lesion assessment and dermoscopy, and adherence to the DERM Instructions for Use and local clinical pathways. Adults 18 years or older with skin lesions suspicious for skin cancer.

DERM's performance depends on the quality of the image provided, correct usage of hardware, and the settings configured on the device. DERM does not provide a definitive diagnosis and does not assess rare malignant lesions not listed in the device's list of possible outputs. DERM should not be used on: patients under age 18, for assessing non-cancer skin conditions (e.g. rashes, eczema, infectious diseases, lupus), for monitoring treatment, for staging disease, for images other than dermoscopic images of skin lesions, for images of skin lesions from anyone other than the identified patient, for open or ulcerated skin lesions, for skin lesions unable to be entirely imaged by the dermatoscope, skin lesions obscured by hair, tattoos or scars, skin lesions beneath nails, in eyes or on mucosal surfaces or on soles of feet or palms of hands, and skin lesions which have previously been biopsied. DERM achieved AUROC of 91.8-95.8% for melanoma detection across different camera devices, with 99.8% negative predictive value (NPV) for correctly excluding melanoma, outperforming dermatologists' NPV of 98.9%. For non-melanoma skin cancers, DERM achieved AUROC of 0.85-0.88 for squamous cell carcinoma and 0.87-0.89 for basal cell carcinoma across multiple devices. In real-world deployment, DERM demonstrated 97% pathway sensitivity for malignant melanoma, exceeding the 95% target rate. In the University of Exeter evaluation, DERM demonstrated its safety, showing high-risk cancer detection rates 26.5% higher than local published rates. 91.8-95.8% 99.8% 0.85-0.88 0.87-0.89 97% +26.5%

DERM has been deployed across patients with all Fitzpatrick skin types (I-VI). Real-world data shows 6-8% of cases assessed had Fitzpatrick type V-VI skin, compared to 4.5% of NHS urgent suspected skin cancer pathway patients from Black, Asian, or mixed ethnicities. DERM correctly identified all melanomas, SCCs, and BCCs in patients with Fitzpatrick V and VI skin types since 2020. Subgroup analysis showed age, skin type, and deprivation did not change the expected distribution of cases assessed by DERM; however it is worth noting that the sample size within subgroups is limited. Darker skin types are underrepresented in the dataset (only 2.2% Fitzpatrick IV-VI in DERM-003 study), limiting generalizability for these populations. DERM cannot currently assess palmoplantar and subungual lesions, which disproportionately affects darker-skinned patients.

The DermaSensor device uses elastic scattering spectroscopy (ESS) and an AI/ML algorithm applied non-invasively to intact skin lesions. It provides results as “Monitor” or “Investigate Further,” with a similarity score for positive results. It is intended to assist physicians, particularly non-dermatologists, with referral decisions and is not a standalone diagnostic tool.

To evaluate skin lesions suggestive of melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, and/or squamous cell carcinoma in patients aged 40 and above to assist referral decisions to a dermatologist. Not a population screening tool or standalone diagnostic. ESS spectral recordings from intact primary skin lesions suspected of melanoma, BCC, or SCC in patients aged 40+. Lesions should not be previously biopsied, recurrent, or metastatic; on scars, tattoos, sunburned skin, or hairy areas; or on palms, soles, mucosal surfaces, genitals, ears, within 1 cm of the eye, or under nails. “Monitor” (negative) or “Investigate Further” (positive), based on analysis of backscattered light spectra by a proprietary ML-derived classifier. For “Investigate Further” results, a Similarity Score of 1–10 is displayed, with higher scores indicating greater similarity to malignant lesions. Adjunctive, software-aided clinical decision support for physicians (including those not trained in dermatology) making referral decisions. It does not replace biopsy, pathology, or physician judgment. Physicians and trained healthcare professionals in clinical settings, including primary care physicians not specialized in dermatology. Patients aged 40+ with lesions suggestive of melanoma, BCC, and/or SCC; primary lesions only, subject to labeled anatomic and clinical exclusions.

Performance has not been specifically evaluated in patients with increased skin-cancer risk (e.g., inherited/drug-induced photosensitivity, genetic predisposition, immune compromise). Not tested on rare skin cancers outside melanoma/BCC/SCC intent. Not for previously biopsied, recurrent, or metastatic lesions; scars, tattoos, sunburned skin, hairy areas; or palms, soles, mucosa, genitals, ears, within 1 cm of the eye, or under nails. In the published validation analysis, dermatologist specificity was higher than device specificity (56.10% vs 26.22%), assuming unbiopsied lesions enrolled by dermatologists were benign.

AI/ML software algorithm using Elastic Scattering Spectroscopy (ESS). Published validation materials describe a final architecture of 10 neural networks trained on different architectures and training-set variations, including a feedforward network and deep networks based on a ResNet-18 architecture adapted for ESS spectral inputs. Published materials describe training on an expansive ESS databank of over 10,000 readings from over 2,000 lesions across multiple health care settings. Prospective, investigator-blinded multicenter clinical validation at 4 U.S. sites enrolled 614 lesions from 394 participants and compared device output with histopathologic evaluation. [Publication](https://www.bu.edu/bmo/files/2024/02/Dermasensor-paper-2.pdf) FDA materials describe the DERM-SUCCESS pivotal clinical study assessing standalone device sensitivity/specificity versus ground-truth diagnosis.

In the published 4-site clinical validation analysis, overall device sensitivity was 97.04% and specificity 26.22%; NPV 89.58% and PPV 57.54%. No statistically significant difference was found between device and dermatologist sensitivity (P = .8203). 97.04% (Published clinical validation cohort) 96.67% (Melanoma, including high-risk melanocytic pathologies) 97.22% (Basal cell carcinoma) 97.01% (Squamous cell carcinoma) 26.22% (Published clinical validation cohort) 89.58% (Published clinical validation cohort) 57.54% (Published clinical validation cohort) 95.5% (FDA review of pivotal study)

SkinVision is an AI-powered mobile app that lets users photograph moles and skin lesions with a smartphone and receive a low/medium/high risk indication to support preventive self-monitoring and decisions about seeking a dermatologist. It combines a clinically validated convolutional neural network algorithm with dermatologist-reviewed training images, and is not intended to provide a diagnosis.

Analyze smartphone photos of skin lesions and classify them with a low/medium/high risk indication to empower self-monitoring and inform decisions about seeking a medical follow-up; not intended as a diagnostic tool. A smartphone photo of a skin lesion captured via the app's guided camera (lesion centered, in focus, area around the mole clear); users can also complete an in-app questionnaire for skin type and risk-factor assessment. A categorical risk indication (low/medium/high) per lesion plus a triage recommendation, generated by a proprietary convolutional neural network trained on dermatologist-reviewed smartphone images; not a diagnostic report. Presented as risk categories with educational explanations to support preventive self-monitoring, not a diagnostic report; a high-risk result prompts a recommendation to seek professional evaluation but does not itself confirm skin cancer. Individuals at risk of developing skin cancer (consumer/self-use), as well as healthcare professionals who may use the output as supplementary information; no clinical knowledge or expertise is required, only a smartphone and the app. General consumers seeking to self-monitor skin lesions for skin cancer risk; not intended for persons under age 18.

Independent studies report sensitivity/specificity varying by evaluation, e.g. 73% sensitivity/83% specificity for melanoma in one study and 95.1% sensitivity/78.3% specificity for (pre)malignant conditions in another; roughly 45% of lesions in one study could not be analyzed by the app; agreement between the app and dermatologists was limited in some evaluations. Sensitivity/specificity estimates vary substantially across studies and between company and independent evaluations; the proprietary training dataset's demographic composition (including skin tone representation) is not publicly disclosed, limiting evaluation of generalizability and equity.

Proprietary convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture for smartphone image-based skin lesion risk assessment. Trained and validated on a proprietary dataset of dermatologist-reviewed smartphone images; one published validation used 131,873 images from 31,449 users (Jan 2016-Aug 2018) rated for risk by dermatologists. Full dataset composition and demographic breakdown are not publicly disclosed. Clinically validated per ISO 14971 risk management and ISO 13485/27001 quality and security standards; reviewed by an independent team of EU-appointed medical technology experts. [Publication](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31494983/) Not disclosed

Reported sensitivity ranges from approximately 73% to over 95% across different independent studies, with specificity varying accordingly (78-83%); company-reported figures tend to be higher than third-party evaluations. One peer-reviewed study found 95.1% sensitivity and 78.3% specificity for detecting (pre)malignant conditions. 95.1% ((pre)malignant conditions, peer-reviewed study) 78.3% ((pre)malignant conditions, peer-reviewed study) 73% (melanoma, independent study)

Full dataset composition is not publicly disclosed; the app is intended for all skin tones and types, but it is unclear whether the proprietary training dataset adequately represents all ethnicities. The company's research pipeline lists 'performance across diverse skin types and demographics' as an ongoing area of work.

Algorithm is continuously updated using newly submitted user images; user data is retained up to 12 months after account deletion. Continuous training and improvement of the algorithm using new sets of submitted images; no fixed release schedule disclosed. support@skinvision.com | https://www.skinvision.com/contact-us

None required for use of the app itself; anyone with a smartphone can use it. Outputs are risk indications and triage recommendations only, not a diagnostic report, and the app explicitly recommends professional evaluation for higher-risk results.

Electronic prescriptions (structured data), clinical notes (unstructured text/PDFs), patient records, payer policy data. Completed PA forms (structured forms), appeal letters (text documents), enrollment forms, patient SMS notifications (text), pharmacy routing instructions, and portal dashboard status updates. Workflow: patient records and prescription data are pulled from the EHR (via integration) or uploaded manually; AI reads clinical documentation and matches it against payer-specific PA requirements and formulary rules; AI auto-generates PA form content within 24 hours; provider reviews and approves the completed PA in the Forus portal; Forus submits to the payer and conducts status follow-ups; if denied, AI analyzes the denial reason and generates an appeal letter drawing on clinical documentation and payer-specific appeal strategies; provider reviews and approves the appeal letter before submission; the system continuously learns from case outcomes. The platform automates administrative work and does not make clinical decisions. Doctors and their staff, including providers of all sizes from 1-2 provider private practices to large physician groups and health systems. Provider must be able to e-prescribe (electronic prescriptions only; Forus does not currently support non-eRx practices). All U.S. patients who are prescribed medications requiring prior authorization. Forus supports every medication, insurance, and pharmacy, including both retail and specialty drugs.
